1.​ Definition

            ●​ Klappvisor Bascinet is a medieval helmet that originated in the 14th century.
               "Klappvisor" is German and translates to "folding visor." The single brow-mounted
               hinge is a distinctive feature of early bascinet visor designs. These bascinet visors
               were often low profile to fit underneath a great helm, but would also serve as a primary
               defense on their own.
            ●​ Klappvisor uses a solid metal visor to protect the face, attached on the forehead by a
               piece of metal, the “spoon”.
            ●​ Klappvisor was used from 1340 to 1400, mainly in Germany and Italy.
            ●​ Klappvisor is approved for 14th century and Transitional armors.
            ●​ Klappvisor is denied for 15th century armors.

3.​ Requirements
         3.1 General Requirements
            ●​ Reproductions must closely resemble the appearance and proportions of a Klappvisor
               source.
            ●​ Any metal part of the helmet must conform to the Armors and weapons Aesthetics and
               decorations document.
            ●​ Any textile or leather part of the helmet must conform to the Textiles and Leather
               document.

         3.2 Visor Requirements
            ●​ Visor must not be too long or too short, it must respect the proportions of historical
               sources.
            ●​ The hinge must be reproduced as per historical sources.
            ●​ It is allowed to weld the hinge. Welded hinges must resemble a functional hinge.
            ●​ It is allowed to weld the visor down. Welded visor must resemble a functional
               removable visor.
            ●​ It is allowed to add a metal plate to protect the throat. Such a plate must be strong
               enough to endure full contact fight and must be concealed under the aventail.
            ●​ A leather strap can be used to secure the visor down.
            ●​ Breath holes should be round and must not exceed a diameter of 10mm. Breath holes
               must not be so numerous that they compromise the helm’s structural integrity. It is
               acceptable to mirror breath holes to both sides.
            ●​ Breath holes of another shape must be documented by historical sources to be
               allowed.


         3.3 Eye-slots
            ●​ Eye slots should resemble sources for the visor.
            ●​ Eye slots should not exceed 25mm tall to prevent any injury.
            ●​ Klappvisor with 2 eye slots are allowed to add up to two (2) safety eye bars per eye
               slot.
            ●​ Klappvisor may have integrated Eye bars. Such eye bars must be made accordingly
               with historical sources, in terms of proportion, numbers and aesthetic.
            ●​ Eye bars must conform to the Eye bars rules document.

         3.4 Aventail
            ●​ Klappvisors must be worn with chainmail aventails, fabric aventails, or scales aventails.
            ●​ Aventails must conform to the Aventails document.
            ●​ Aventails must be attached to the bascinet by a system of leather and vervelles.




Helmet Klappvisors                                                                    7

●​ The aventail must be fastened down to the edge of a padded pelerine attached to the
               helmet liner.
            ●​ Protective plates covering the cervical spine must be hidden under the aventail.

         3.5 Others
            ●​ Klappvisors may be decorated in the spirit of medieval styles, such as orle, torse,
               decorated aventails (with cooper/brass chainmail rings), vervelle covers and coat of
               arms badges etc.
            ●​ Such decoration must be made in coherence with historical sources.
            ●​ Using modern and/or offensive imagery and slogans is prohibited.
